title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models
authors: Louenas Zemmour, Xavier Gloerfelt, Paola Cinnella
abstract: Laminar-turbulent transition governs skin friction, heat transfer and losses in turbomachinery, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models rely on empirical correlations and hand-calibrated activation functions whose structural deficiencies cannot be resolved by recalibration. We propose a CFD-driven sparse symbolic regression framework to learn interpretable, closed-form corrections to the production and destruction activation functions in the intermittency equation of the local, Galilean-invariant $k$-$ω$-$γ$ model of Ge et al. Each correction combines a polynomial of a local pressure-gradient parameter, controlling amplitude and sign, with a bounded exponential of local flow features, controlling spatial support. This construction bounds the corrections without ad hoc limiters. Coefficients are identified by gradient-free optimization with the RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates, using mean-velocity data from wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate cases. Elastic-net hyperparameters are selected automatically through bi-level optimization with leave-one-case-out cross-validation. The resulting model retains 11 of 21 candidate terms, compared with 20 under conventional grid-search tuning, while achieving comparable or slightly better accuracy on training and unseen cases. Both approaches recover the same leading-order correction. Applied without retraining to the transonic LS89 turbine cascade, far beyond the training envelope, the augmented model remains numerically robust and improves heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70% where the baseline predicts premature transition under high freestream turbulence. Residual errors in transition onset and length highlight the limits of training on flat-plate data alone.

infographic.key_insight: CFD-driven symbolic regression learns compact, interpretable corrections to a RANS transition model that improve predictions beyond the flat-plate training cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate transition modeling can improve turbine heat-transfer and loss predictions, with heat-transfer errors reduced by up to 70% in the tested LS89 cascade cases.
method: Learn bounded, closed-form corrections to production and destruction activation functions in the k–ω–γ intermittency equation.
Optimize coefficients with a RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates.
Select elastic-net hyperparameters through bi-level optimization and leave-one-case-out validation, retaining 11 of 21 candidate terms.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training used wall-resolved LES mean-velocity data for ERCOFTAC T3 flat plates; testing without retraining improved LS89 turbine heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points.
infographic.watch_item: Residual errors in transition onset and length indicate that flat-plate-only training limits accuracy in more complex turbine flows.
infographic.paper_title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
authors: Semih Kacmaz, E. A. Huerta
abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.

infographic.key_insight: Learned surrogates emulate 3D resistive MHD turbulence, with UNet and transformer models achieving relative velocity errors of 0.018–0.053 over about one large-eddy turnover time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models offer a route toward lower-cost plasma turbulence simulation while preserving current sheets, energy spectra and other key flow diagnostics.
method: Compare a convolutional UNet, shifted-window transformer and Fourier neural operator as autoregressive emulators.
Train on 128³ decaying MHD simulations at Reynolds numbers 1000, 3000 and 6000.
Use two-stage training—single steps followed by short rollouts—with a shared stopping rule.
infographic.evidence_signal: Training uses 500 simulations per Reynolds number; public-benchmark evaluations report 39% lower error than the best published FactFormer-set model and one-third to one-half lower rollout errors than The Well's best baselines.

infographic.paper_title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence

title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)
authors: Miranda J S Horne, Peter K Jimack, Amirul Khan, He Wang
abstract: Physics informed machine learning provides a framework to study and simulate fluid dynamics, potentially at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional numerical methods, with the goal of improving the explainability, accuracy and robustness of purely data driven machine learning methods. In this work, we extend the hard constraint projection (HCP) method developed by Chen et al. [Journal of Computational Physics, 445, 110624, 2021] from a linear partial differential equation (PDE) to a nonlinear PDE: the 1D Burgers' equation. To strictly impose a discrete approximation of the governing equation, the Burgers' equation is first locally discretised (using a finite difference stencil) then decomposed into a constraint matrix and a prediction matrix. Using tools from linear algebra, the constraint matrix is used to construct a projection matrix. A physics informed neural network (PINN) [Raissi et al. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686, 2019] is used to predict the velocity, and a final unlearnable layer projects the velocity prediction to the hyperplane of exact solutions to a discretised form of the Burgers' equation. Our initial results indicate that the HCP-PINN initially trains similarly to an equivalent PINN, and as the PINN loss plateaus, the HCP-PINN loss continues to decline. When tested on a previously unseen uniform grid of points covering the domain, the HCP-PINN exhibits higher accuracy, converging to a data error approximately an order of magnitude lower than the comparable PINN. We also observe that the inclusion of the HCP layer results in better observance of the governing PDE. Our findings suggest that the HCP-PINN can be more robust to the selection of physics collocation points, and less dependent on collocation point quantity.

infographic.key_insight: A fixed hard-constraint projection layer improves a PINN’s accuracy by enforcing a local discrete approximation of the nonlinear 1D Burgers’ equation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hard-constraint projection could make physics-informed fluid models more reliable and less sensitive to the number and placement of physics collocation points.
method: Locally discretise Burgers’ equation with a finite-difference stencil.
Decompose the discrete equation into constraint and prediction matrices to construct a projection.
Apply a final non-trainable layer that projects PINN velocity predictions onto the discrete constraint hyperplane.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an unseen uniform grid, initial experiments report approximately one order of magnitude lower data error than a comparable PINN, alongside better PDE adherence.
infographic.watch_item: Exact enforcement applies to the local discrete approximation, not the continuous PDE; evidence is limited to initial 1D Burgers’ experiments.
infographic.paper_title: Hard Constraint Projection in a Physics Informed Neural Network (Burgers)

title: Learned Warm Starts for Steady Transonic RANS Simulations of Wing and Aircraft Configurations
authors: Muhammad Irfan Zafar, Saleh Abuhanieh, Şahin Yiğit
abstract: Neural surrogates can accelerate many-query aerodynamic analyses, but their standalone predictions may be insufficiently accurate or robust to support reliable design evaluations. We develop a learned warm-start formulation that predicts mean-flow and turbulence fields directly on native CFD meshes for subsequent correction by the RANS solver. A common architecture and objective structure are used across subcritical and transonic flows, including challenging conditions with shock-induced separation. A condition-modulated Transolver combines Fourier and wall features with target-gated regularization, a Sobolev-type loss, adaptive loss weighting and sampled training. Prediction requires no preliminary flow solution, and training requires no solver-residual evaluation. Extensive 3D CFD evaluations on SuperWing, the NASA Common Research Model (CRM) and DLR-F6 assess geometric and operating-condition generalization, including interpolation, extrapolation and cross-mesh deployment, using Spalart-Allmaras and $k$-$ω$ SST closures on million-cell meshes. Unseen nominal cases achieve geometric-mean iteration speed-ups of approximately $2$-$4\times$ under a common convergence criterion based on cold-run aerodynamic coefficients. On CRM, learned initialization provides greater aggregate acceleration than nearest-condition restarts using the same solution library. Resolution invariance enables direct deployment of coarse-mesh models on finer meshes without retraining, solution interpolation or target-condition coarse solves. Including data generation and training, estimated campaign speed-ups reach $2.1$-$2.3\times$. No warm run diverges; fewer than $2\%$ fail to satisfy the cold-reference convergence criterion. These results support learned initialization for repeated aerodynamic analyses, while highlighting initialization sensitivity near separation as a remaining limitation.

infographic.key_insight: Learned flow-field initialization accelerates steady RANS convergence by approximately 2–4× in iterations on unseen nominal cases while retaining CFD solver correction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Warm starts can reduce repeated aerodynamic analysis costs, with estimated campaign speed-ups of 2.1–2.3× including data generation and training.
method: A condition-modulated Transolver predicts mean-flow and turbulence fields directly on native CFD meshes.
Training combines Fourier and wall features, target-gated regularization, Sobolev-type loss and adaptive loss weighting without solver-residual evaluation.

infographic.watch_item: Initialization remains sensitive near flow separation, and iteration reductions do not directly equal end-to-end runtime savings.
infographic.paper_title: Learned Warm Starts for Steady Transonic RANS Simulations of Wing and Aircraft Configurations

title: Physics-Informed Latent Neural ODEs for Reduced-Order Modeling of Hydrogen, Ammonia, and Methane Combustion Kinetics
authors: Jay Patel, Shubhangi Bansude
abstract: Detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms are computationally expensive in reacting-flow simulations because of their high dimensionality and numerical stiffness. We develop an end-to-end physics-informed autoencoder neural ordinary differential equation (PI-AE-NODE) framework in which an encoder compresses the thermochemical state into a low-dimensional latent space, a Neural ODE advances it continuously in time, and a decoder reconstructs the temperature and all species mass fractions. Elemental conservation, mass conservation, and enthalpy consistency are embedded in the training objective. The framework is applied to H$_2$/air, NH$_3$/air, and CH$_4$/air autoignition using detailed mechanisms of increasing size and complexity, which are represented accurately with only a few latent variables. Compared with an otherwise identical data-driven model, the physical constraints improve ignition delay prediction and conservation behaviour. The models reproduce major and intermediate species evolution at both training and unseen conditions, and their latent dynamics permit efficient explicit integration, with the computational advantage over the detailed mechanisms increasing with mechanism size.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed latent Neural ODEs reduce combustion kinetics to a few latent variables while improving ignition-delay prediction and conservation over an otherwise identical data-driven model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a route to cheaper chemical-kinetics integration in reacting-flow simulations, with reported computational advantages increasing as mechanism size grows.
method: Encode temperature and species mass fractions into a low-dimensional latent state.
Advance latent dynamics with a Neural ODE and decode the full thermochemical state.
Train with elemental conservation, mass conservation, and enthalpy-consistency constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on H₂/air, NH₃/air, and CH₄/air autoignition shows reproduction of major and intermediate species at training and unseen conditions, with efficient explicit latent integration.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract establishes autoignition performance but does not demonstrate robustness in coupled turbulent reacting-flow simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Latent Neural ODEs for Reduced-Order Modeling of Hydrogen, Ammonia, and Methane Combustion Kinetics

title: Optimizing synthetic jet placement for control stability in increasing Reynolds number flows based on deep reinforcement learning
authors: Wang Jia, Hang Xu
abstract: This study utilizes reinforcement learning algorithms to develop advanced control strategies for manipulating synthetic jets positioned on a cylinder, aiming to achieve effective flow control. It addresses critical challenges in achieving robust performance across moderate to high Reynolds numbers (Re) and varying jet placement configurations. The results demonstrate that placing synthetic jets near flow separation regions yields optimal control performance. At Re = 500, the multi-objective flow control strategy achieves up to 37.4% drag reduction and 99% suppression of lift oscillations, while completely suppressing vortex shedding. At Re = 1,000, drag reduction improves to 49.1%, with equally effective lift suppression and complete vortex shedding suppression. At Re = 2,000, the strategy achieves a maximum drag reduction of 58.8% and suppresses 90% of lift oscillations, although some residual wake instabilities persist. Additionally, synthetic jets effectively disrupted detached vortices and stabilized the wake, resulting in streamlined flow and suppressed vortex shedding. These findings underscore the pivotal influence of jet placement in optimizing flow control efficacy, while affirming the advanced capability of control strategies to tackle intricate challenges.

infographic.key_insight: Deep reinforcement learning controls cylinder-mounted synthetic jets most effectively near flow separation regions, reducing drag and suppressing lift oscillations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing jet placement could improve active flow-control performance and stability across increasing Reynolds numbers.
method: Use deep reinforcement learning to control cylinder-mounted synthetic jets.
Evaluate jet placement configurations across Reynolds numbers of 500, 1,000, and 2,000.
Apply multi-objective control targeting drag reduction and lift-oscillation suppression.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports drag reductions up to 37.4%, 49.1%, and 58.8% at Re = 500, 1,000, and 2,000, respectively, with complete vortex-shedding suppression at the two lower Reynolds numbers.
infographic.watch_item: Residual wake instabilities persist at Re = 2,000, so stability beyond the tested conditions remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Optimizing synthetic jet placement for control stability in increasing Reynolds number flows based on deep reinforcement learning

title: Bistability in the stalling behavior of thick, cambered airfoils under elevated freestream turbulence
authors: Jaylon E. McGhee, John A. N. Farnsworth
abstract: The aerodynamic performance of a thick, cambered FFA-W3-301 airfoil section near and beyond stall was examined under elevated freestream turbulence using time-resolved surface pressure measurements for chord-based Reynolds numbers from 125,000 to 275,000. Three passive turbulence grids were used to isolate the effects of turbulence intensity and integral length scale, and the results were compared with a clean inflow. The elevated turbulence largely had a positive effect on the mean performance of the airfoil section, eliminating premature flow separation and recovering lift and drag polars more representative of a higher effective Reynolds number; however, resolving the lift in time showed that the time-averaged polars concealed bistable switching. The time-averaged lift was an occupancy-weighted average of two states, and conventional mean and standard-deviation statistics misrepresented the true post-stall unsteady loads. Beyond the maximum-lift angle of attack, the lift alternated repeatedly between two distinct levels with no characteristic frequency. At the highest tested Reynolds number, the switching persisted over an angle-of-attack range of up to nine degrees, more than an order of magnitude wider than that reported for a thin, symmetric section in a low turbulence inflow. The lift levels of the two states were also found to be nearly independent of the inflow turbulence level, whereas the fraction of time spent in each differed between turbulence conditions. conditionally averaged surface pressure distributions and proper orthogonal decomposition of the surface pressure consistently showed that neither state is fully attached; the states correspond to two positions of a single separation front on the suction side, a switching accurately captured by a single pressure mode from the decomposition.

infographic.key_insight: Elevated freestream turbulence improves mean airfoil performance but masks bistable post-stall switching between two partially separated flow states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Post-stall load assessment should account for state switching and occupancy rather than relying only on mean lift and standard deviation.
method: Measured time-resolved surface pressures on a thick, cambered FFA-W3-301 airfoil at Reynolds numbers of 125,000–275,000.
Compared clean inflow with three passive turbulence grids to separate turbulence-intensity and integral-length-scale effects.
Used conditional pressure averages and proper orthogonal decomposition to identify separation-front states.
infographic.evidence_signal: At the highest tested Reynolds number, switching persisted across up to 9° of angle of attack, with nearly turbulence-independent lift levels but different state occupancies.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern one airfoil section over a limited Reynolds-number range; transfer to full-scale, three-dimensional wings requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Bistability in the stalling behavior of thick, cambered airfoils under elevated freestream turbulence

title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures
authors: James Malcolm, Clare McColgan, Emma Mullarkey, Emad Chaparian
abstract: We develop a computational framework to investigate the flow kinematics of viscoplastic materials, described by the Herschel-Bulkley model, in vane-in-cup rheometers. Numerical simulations are performed using augmented Lagrangian finite element and regularised finite volume methods for two- and three-dimensional configurations, respectively, to characterise the hydrodynamics and yielding behaviour over a broad range of effective parameters. Three types of vanes are investigated: conventional 4- and 6-arm bespoke vanes and a 24-arm fractal vane (Owens et al., J. Rheol., vol. 64(3), 2020, 643-662). Our previous two-dimensional study (Chaparian et al., J. Non-Newtonian Fluid Mech., vol. 307, 2022, 104857) demonstrated the superiority of the fractal vane over conventional N-arm designs. The bespoke vanes produce highly non-uniform yielding, leading to significant deviations from the circular Couette analogy, whereas the 24-arm fractal vane generates nearly axisymmetric yield surfaces that effectively "cloak" the vane geometry. Consequently, the resulting flow closely resembles the azimuthal shear in a conventional "bob & cup" rheometer, providing substantially more accurate rheological measurements. Building on these findings, the present study revisits the torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain rate conversions used in vane-in-cup rheometry. In particular, we re-examine the circular Couette analogy that underpins both the physical interpretation of the flow and the extraction of flow curves from raw rheometric data. Based on our extensive two- and three-dimensional simulations, we identify limitations of the existing conversion relations and propose improved closure expressions that enable more accurate determination of material's rheological properties. Furthermore, the three-dimensional flow structures and yielding patterns within the vane-in-cup fixtures are characterised.

infographic.key_insight: Computational rheometry supports improved vane-in-cup conversion relations, with the 24-arm fractal vane producing nearly axisymmetric yielding that better approximates circular Couette flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improved torque-to-stress and rotation-to-strain-rate conversions can make rheological measurements of yield-stress materials more accurate.
method: Model viscoplastic fluids using the Herschel–Bulkley constitutive law.
Simulate 2D flow with augmented Lagrangian finite elements and 3D flow with regularised finite volumes.
Compare conventional 4- and 6-arm vanes with a 24-arm fractal vane.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive 2D and 3D simulations across a broad parameter range, but provides no quantitative accuracy gains or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Circular Couette conversions can be inaccurate for non-axisymmetric yielding; revised closures require validation for the intended geometry and operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Three-dimensional computational rheometry of viscoplastic fluids in vane-in-cup fixtures

title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization
authors: Siva Viknesh, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: High-Péclet-number transport problems give rise to thin boundary layers with steep near-wall gradients whose accurate solution requires high-resolution meshes and could challenge inverse modeling. To address this challenge, we develop an overlapping Schwarz domain-decomposition framework grounded in perturbation theory, in which an inner equation governs near-wall dynamics and an outer equation governs bulk transport, and both subproblems are discretized using the finite element method and assembled into a fully differentiable multidomain physics solver. The formulation permits coarser mesh resolutions, reducing computational cost relative to a single-domain formulation. Exploiting the differentiability of the coupled solver, we formulate inverse problems in which the governing equations and boundary conditions are imposed as hard constraints, with the Schwarz coupling enforcing interface continuity. To accelerate the resulting adjoint-based optimization, we integrate large language models (LLMs) into the inverse workflow in two distinct configurations: a standalone optimizer that proposes successive parameter updates from the adjoint-computed sensitivities and an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) approach with access to the complete solver workflow, enabling it to perform multistage optimization procedures. The agentic AI configuration is shown to be most advantageous when the spatially varying unknown is represented in a functional basis rather than a high-dimensional nodal field representation. In this case, the AI agent grows the library of candidate basis functions during optimization under a prescribed admission policy, admitting predefined families in stages and initializing their parameters. In short, our proposed framework integrates Schwarz-coupled differentiable physics with agentic AI optimization for the inverse modeling of multiscale transport problems.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable Schwarz-coupled solver combines near-wall and bulk transport models to support inverse modeling of thin boundary layers, with agentic AI guiding optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can reduce mesh requirements and computational cost for high-Péclet transport while enforcing governing equations and boundary conditions as hard constraints.
method: Discretize perturbation-based inner and outer transport equations with finite elements.
Couple overlapping domains through differentiable Schwarz iterations that enforce interface continuity.
Use adjoint sensitivities for optimization, with an AI agent staging optimization and expanding an admissible functional basis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reduced computational cost versus a single-domain formulation and greater agentic AI advantage for functional-basis unknowns than for high-dimensional nodal fields, but provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Agentic optimization benefits appear representation-dependent; performance on high-dimensional nodal unknowns requires careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Differentiable Schwarz-Coupled Solvers for Thin Boundary Layer Transport: Inverse Modeling via Agentic AI Optimization

title: Dual-Band Mid-Infrared Imaging for Measurement of Fuel Concentration and Temperature in a Supersonic Cavity
authors: Loren C. Hahn, Erik L. Braun, Brendan J. McGann, Katherine C. Opacich, Timothy M. Ombrello
abstract: A dual-band mid-infrared absorption imaging method is demonstrated for spatially resolved measurement of ethylene concentration and temperature in a Mach-2 cavity flow. The method used narrowband filters selected to exploit the differing in-band temperature sensitivities of ethylene absorption, together with a broadband infrared source and high-frame-rate mid-wave infrared camera. Temperature-dependent, filter-weighted absorption cross-sections were used to measure two-dimensional ethylene number density and temperature fields. Measurements were obtained for cavity, curtain, and discrete fuel-injection configurations, including cases with the leading edge of a quasi-steady shock near the cavity. Cavity equivalence ratio measurements agreed well with independent extractive measurements and reproduced trends previously observed using hyperspectral imaging. A complementary single-band implementation using a temperature-independent filter provided instantaneous ethylene concentration fields at 100 Hz and revealed intermittent reductions in cavity equivalence ratio associated with plume deflection by the shock train leading edge. The dual-band approach provides quantitative full-field measurements with substantially simpler spectral instrumentation than hyperspectral imaging while retaining flexibility for time-resolved flow measurements.

infographic.key_insight: Dual-band mid-infrared absorption imaging maps ethylene concentration and temperature in a Mach-2 cavity using simpler spectral instrumentation than hyperspectral imaging.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spatially resolved fuel and temperature measurements help diagnose supersonic fuel mixing and shock-driven changes in cavity fueling.
method: Pair a broadband infrared source and high-frame-rate camera with two narrowband filters having different temperature sensitivities.
Use temperature-dependent, filter-weighted absorption cross-sections to infer two-dimensional ethylene number density and temperature.
Use a complementary temperature-independent single-band filter for instantaneous concentration imaging at 100 Hz.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across cavity, curtain, and discrete injection configurations, cavity equivalence ratios agreed well with independent extractive measurements, while single-band imaging revealed intermittent fueling reductions associated with shock-induced plume deflection.
infographic.watch_item: The reported 100 Hz concentration measurements used the single-band implementation; equivalent time-resolved dual-band temperature performance is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Dual-Band Mid-Infrared Imaging for Measurement of Fuel Concentration and Temperature in a Supersonic Cavity

title: Triadic energy cascades and linear amplification mechanisms in supersonic turbulent boundary layers over curved walls
authors: Lucas Feitosa de Souza, Hugo F. da Silva Lui, William Roberto Wolf, Pedro Stefanin Volpiani
abstract: Direct numerical simulations are performed to investigate supersonic turbulent boundary layers subjected to continuous concave and convex surface curvatures. Scale-resolved spectral turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budgets, triadic energy-transfer bispectra, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), and global resolvent analysis are employed to elucidate the effects of compressibility and pressure gradients, and to distinguish the linear and nonlinear mechanisms at play. Over concave walls, the destabilizing curvature enhances pressure-strain redistribution, shifting near-wall turbulence toward a two-component state, and induces a shear-driven outer-layer production peak at low spanwise wavenumbers. Bispectral and SPOD analyses reveal that this outer-layer energy feeds a structured, multi-step triadic transfer toward fundamental large-scale and spanwise-uniform modes, which physically manifests as streamwise vortex breakdown rather than a three-dimensional inverse cascade. Global resolvent analysis further demonstrates that while nonlinear triadic interactions select the dominant scale amplitudes, the spatial topology of these coherent structures is dictated by linear mean-flow receptivity and spatially developing convective instabilities. Conversely, over convex walls, stabilizing curvature and dilatation attenuate pressure fluctuations and suppress pressure-strain redistribution, breaking the near-wall turbulent cycle and trapping energy within elongated, one-component streamwise streaks, while a localized resolvent wavemaker energizes the downstream recovery region.

infographic.key_insight: Wall curvature reorganizes supersonic turbulence: concave walls promote multi-step triadic energy transfers and vortex breakdown, while convex walls suppress redistribution and retain energy in elongated streamwise streaks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Separating nonlinear scale selection from linear flow-structure amplification can inform turbulence modeling for curved supersonic surfaces.
method: Direct numerical simulations of supersonic boundary layers over concave and convex walls.
Scale-resolved TKE budgets, triadic-transfer bispectra, and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition.
Global resolvent analysis to identify linear receptivity and convective amplification.
infographic.evidence_signal: DNS-based diagnostics identify a concave-wall outer-layer production peak at low spanwise wavenumbers and convex-wall suppression of pressure fluctuations and pressure-strain redistribution.
infographic.watch_item: Generality across Mach numbers, Reynolds numbers, and curvature strengths is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Triadic energy cascades and linear amplification mechanisms in supersonic turbulent boundary layers over curved walls

title: Agentic AI Reasoning and Learned Sampling for Task-Aware Projection Selection in Sparse-View CT: Predicting Hemodynamics
authors: Mahmoud Elhadidy, Roshan M. D'Souza, Amirhossein Arzani
abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces the number of acquired projections, but conventional sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference. Here, we investigate optimal task-aware projection selection for directly predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography (CTA) measurements. Using computational fluid dynamics simulations of intracranial aneurysms, we generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections and train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) to predict two targets: the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. The FNO was coupled with optimal input selection for simultaneous optimal sampling and training. Our goal was to investigate if agentic AI could discover optimal sampling strategies that outperform current methods. We compared fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling with three task-aware optimal selection strategies: Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method, and an agentic AI selector. The methods were compared at different view selection budgets. A detailed analysis of the AI agent was performed to understand its reasoning and performance. For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors (Agentic performs slightly better) and substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimized selection becomes important at extremely sparse acquisitions. Analysis of the selected masks reveals multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions. Moreover, masks optimized for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions, showing that task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition. This work suggests the possibility of designing sparse acquisitions directly around downstream physical quantities.

infographic.key_insight: Task-aware CT projection selection improves direct hemodynamic prediction under extreme sparsity, but the selected views can be poor for image reconstruction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sparse CT acquisition could be tailored to wall shear stress prediction rather than anatomical reconstruction alone.
method: Generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections from CFD simulations of intracranial aneurysms.
Train a Fourier neural operator to predict spatially resolved and spatially averaged time-averaged wall shear stress.
Compare uniform and golden-angle sampling with Gumbel-Softmax, Soft top-K, and agentic AI selection across view budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic CFD-derived data, agentic AI and Soft top-K achieved the lowest mean errors for spatially resolved wall shear stress, with agentic AI slightly better and both substantially outperforming fixed sampling under extreme sparsity.
infographic.watch_item: Validation on real clinical CTA is needed, and views optimized for hemodynamic prediction may not support adequate image reconstruction.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI Reasoning and Learned Sampling for Task-Aware Projection Selection in Sparse-View CT: Predicting Hemodynamics

title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
authors: Krishan Chand, Ahmad Peyvan, Haoxiang Luo
abstract: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

infographic.key_insight: Non-dimensionalization can determine PINN trainability: free-fall scaling avoids the large buoyancy coefficient that drives gradient imbalance under thermal-diffusive scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing physically appropriate scaling before training can improve PINN heat-transfer predictions for buoyancy-driven engineering flows.
method: Compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall scalings under identical training conditions.
Study a differentially heated square cavity at Pr = 0.71 and Ra = 10³–10⁵.
Measure loss gradients and test sparse-data supervision and adaptive loss weighting.
infographic.evidence_signal: Free-fall scaling achieved mean Nusselt-number errors below 1.1% for Ra ≤ 10⁴, while diffusive scaling produced 157–650% errors and diverged at Ra = 10⁵.
infographic.watch_item: Free-fall scaling still missed the transient Nusselt-number overshoot in unsteady convection, despite accurately predicting long-time heat transfer.
infographic.paper_title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training

title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium
authors: Jose Antonio Lara Benitez, Kareem Hegazy, Anastasis Kratsios, Ivan Dokmanić, Maarten V. de Hoop, Michael W. Mahoney
abstract: The ability to emulate complicated and computationally-expensive physical systems in an efficient and stable manner is a popular motivation for scientific machine learning (SciML). Stable numerical solvers tend to be computationally expensive, as they attempt to resolve small (spatial and temporal) scales that receive and dissipate spectral energy. Learned coarse-grid forecasters remove the dissipative channel, allowing unresolved frequencies to re-emerge as grid-scale noise (aliasing). In this paper, we use the Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) method to explore stable emulation at extremely coarse grids, demonstrating physically-principled control over entropy dynamics that reinforces the physical system's dissipative mechanism. Entropically-stabilized NeurDE produces stable long-time rollouts for thousands of forecasting steps on large Reynolds number turbulent flows ($\mathrm{Re}=100{,}000$) with very coarse grids (down to $\mathbb{R}^{16\times16}$). At these very coarse grid scales, entropically-stabilized NeurDE can be more stable than even our stabilized data-generation numerical method.

infographic.key_insight: Entropically stabilized Neural Discrete Equilibrium (NeurDE) enables stable, long-time turbulent-flow emulation on extremely coarse grids by reinforcing physical dissipation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support efficient coarse-grid turbulence forecasting while reducing instability from unresolved small-scale dynamics.
method: Use NeurDE to emulate fluid dynamics on coarse grids.
Control entropy dynamics to reinforce the system’s dissipative mechanism.
Suppress instability associated with unresolved frequencies and grid-scale aliasing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports stable rollouts over thousands of forecasting steps at Re = 100,000 on grids as coarse as 16×16, with stability sometimes exceeding the stabilized data-generation solver.
infographic.watch_item: Long-time stability alone does not establish accuracy of turbulent statistics; the abstract does not quantify that fidelity.
infographic.paper_title: Learning the Entropic Relaxation: Stable Coarse-Grid Emulation with Neural Discrete Equilibrium

title: Pore-scale mechanisms of capillary imbibition in cement-based materials revealed by direct numerical simulations in a realistic FIB-SEM microstructure
authors: Luka Malenica, Zhidong Zhang, Ueli Angst
abstract: Moisture transport in cement-based materials involves transient multiphase flow through highly irregular pore networks, where evolving air--water interfaces strongly influence liquid invasion and gas displacement. Here, pore-resolved, image-based direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to investigate spontaneous imbibition in a FIB--SEM-reconstructed cementitious microstructure, resolving air--water interface dynamics at nanometre-to-micrometre spatial scales and nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. As these dynamics remain inaccessible to direct experimental observation at such scales, the simulations provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first direct view of transient imbibition within the capillary porosity of a realistic cementitious microstructure. The three-dimensional simulations reveal highly heterogeneous wetting-front propagation, continuous interface reconfiguration, and progressive air entrapment, showing that local dynamics depend on evolving interface curvature and capillary-pressure fields rather than on characteristic pore size alone. Significant air entrapment develops even within the capillary pores and under perfectly water-wetting conditions, progressively reducing the saturation rate, while the capillary pressure of trapped-air clusters depends strongly on local interface geometry rather than gas volume alone. Controlled two-dimensional analyses show that the balance between capillary, viscous, inertial, and gravitational effects is strongly scale-dependent. Comparison with the three-dimensional simulations highlights the importance of out-of-plane interface curvature and pore-network connectivity. The framework also resolves moisture conditions at the steel--concrete interface, illustrating its potential for corrosion-relevant pore-scale analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Imbibition in realistic cement pores is governed by evolving interface geometry and connectivity, with trapped air slowing saturation even under perfectly water-wetting conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Resolving pore-scale water invasion can inform moisture-transport assessment and corrosion-relevant analysis at steel–concrete interfaces.
method: Pore-resolved, multiphase DNS in a 3D FIB–SEM-reconstructed cementitious microstructure.
Resolve transient air–water interfaces from nanometre-to-micrometre spatial scales.
Use controlled 2D analyses to examine scale-dependent force balances.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 3D simulations reveal heterogeneous wetting fronts and progressive air entrapment, while comparison with 2D analyses highlights out-of-plane curvature and network connectivity.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no direct experimental validation of the resolved transient interfaces, which remain experimentally inaccessible at these scales.
infographic.paper_title: Pore-scale mechanisms of capillary imbibition in cement-based materials revealed by direct numerical simulations in a realistic FIB-SEM microstructure

title: Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods on Quantum Hardware
authors: Melvina Quartey, Lucy T. Zhang
abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods encounter significant computational bottlenecks in large systems and at high Reynolds number flows due to the rapid increase in degrees of freedom, even on flagship supercomputers. As quantum computers emerge, the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has been proposed as a quantum-native alternative for solving fluid dynamics problems. However, until recently, nearly all studies have relied on classical quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware. This study presents a benchmark of a one-dimensional QLBM implementation executed on three different IBM Quantum hardware. We design and test a quantum circuit for the advection-diffusion equation using amplitude encoding, a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK)-type collision operator, and a streaming step with periodic boundary conditions. Our numerical experiments evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate count, total circuit depth, runtime, and accuracy metrics including maximum absolute error ($L_\infty$ norm) and root-mean-square error (RMSE). We find that the present collision and streaming operators dominate the overall cost and become the primary scalability bottleneck on current hardware. To mitigate the prohibitive cost of full quantum state tomography on hardware-based benchmarking exercises, we introduce a sampler-based measurement strategy that reconstructs macroscopic density fields directly from computational-basis measurements. This approach substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics on hardware. These results provide a quantitative assessment of QLBM performance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime and identify the principal algorithmic and experimental limitations that must be addressed for QLBM to become viable for fluid dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Hardware benchmarks of one-dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann show that collision and streaming dominate circuit cost, while sampler-based density reconstruction reduces measurement overhead.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study identifies practical barriers to quantum fluid simulation without establishing a computational advantage over classical CFD.
method: Encode a one-dimensional advection–diffusion problem in quantum amplitudes.
Apply BGK-type collision and periodic-boundary streaming operators.
Reconstruct macroscopic density from computational-basis samples instead of full state tomography.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on three IBM Quantum devices evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate counts, circuit depth, runtime, maximum absolute error, and RMSE, with sampler-based reconstruction preserving expected advection–diffusion dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to a one-dimensional benchmark, and collision and streaming costs remain scalability bottlenecks on current noisy hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods on Quantum Hardware

title: Jovian Polar Vortex Generation in a Shallow-Water Model with Quasi-Stochastic Convection
authors: Yuhang Ruan, Hao Fu, Cheng Li, Da Yang
abstract: The mechanisms governing the formation and maintenance of polar vortices on Saturn and Jupiter represent a significant challenge in current planetary atmospheric dynamics. In the presence of internal heat sources, the existence of condensable components leads to widespread moist convection in the polar regions of these gas giants. However, the role of moist convective organization in the formation and maintenance of such polar vortices remains poorly understood. To investigate the interaction between convection and polar vortices, this study develops a polar $γ$-plane shallow-water model coupled with a quasi-stochastic convective parameterization. In this quasi-stochastic scheme, convection is prescribed as localized impulsive mass sinks, with the inception probability depending on local vorticity, thereby assigning a higher convective likelihood to cyclonic regions. Numerical experiments successfully reproduce shielded cyclones and persistent vortex crystals reminiscent of Jupiter's polar configuration. Increasing mesoscale feedback promotes vortex growth, shield formation, and spectral organization, while the characteristic vortex scale depends on both the deformation radius and the convective parameterization. The resulting patterns exhibit both clockwise and counterclockwise structural drift, whose direction and rate are not adequately captured by a conventional Rossby wave phase-speed estimate. A Biot--Savart diagnostic reveals competing contributions to structural drift, with predominantly counterclockwise advection induced by the other vortices and clockwise advection induced by the background vorticity outside the identified vortices. These results provide a possible formation pathway for shielded vortex crystals and highlight the role of convective feedback in vortex formation.

infographic.key_insight: Vorticity-dependent convective feedback can generate shielded cyclones and persistent vortex crystals resembling Jupiter’s polar configuration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a simplified framework for studying how localized convective forcing organizes large-scale rotating flows.
method: Simulate polar dynamics with a γ-plane shallow-water model.
Represent convection as localized impulsive mass sinks, more likely in cyclonic regions.
Use a Biot–Savart diagnostic to separate vortex and background contributions to structural drift.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments reproduce persistent vortex crystals and show that stronger mesoscale feedback promotes vortex growth, shielding, and spectral organization.
infographic.watch_item: Vortex scale depends on both deformation radius and convective parameterization, so quantitative predictions require careful parameter sensitivity assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Jovian Polar Vortex Generation in a Shallow-Water Model with Quasi-Stochastic Convection

title: Dynamics of a two-dimensional microswimmer near a slippery boundary
authors: Takahiro Kanazawa, Darren Crowdy
abstract: Microswimmers near walls and interfaces can switch between qualitatively different modes of motion depending on the slip properties of the neighbouring boundaries. To study this theoretically, a two-dimensional point-singularity model of a microswimmer, which does not self-propel in unbounded fluid, is placed near a flat viscosity discontinuity between two fluids with viscosity ratio $σ$, and also near a partial-slip wall with Navier-slip length $λ$. Using complex-variable methods, the dynamical systems governing the swimmer motion are derived explicitly in both scenarios. Near the viscosity discontinuity, below a universal critical viscosity ratio $σ_c=1/2$, the swimmer is trapped at a fixed height with its stresslet axis normal to the boundary. When $σ=σ_c$ it glides parallel to the boundary at a speed selected by its orientation, with a terminal speed determined by its initial state. For $σ>σ_c$ it oscillates periodically in height and orientation while drifting along the boundary. The dynamics near a partial-slip wall depend on the ratio of the slip length to the length scale of the singularity and are similar in exhibiting an analogous transition at a critical slip length. It is found, however, that the dynamics near a viscosity discontinuity for $σ$ above $σ_c$ are richer than those near the partial-slip boundary, including the existence of a hydrodynamic bound state with zero net displacement over one period. Although the study is limited to two dimensions, these results show how a single boundary parameter organises qualitatively distinct modes of locomotion, in close analogy with slip-induced transitions reported for three-dimensional swimmers.

infographic.key_insight: Boundary slip properties organise a non-self-propelling 2D model microswimmer into trapped, gliding or oscillatory motion, with a universal transition at viscosity ratio σ = 1/2.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tuning fluid viscosity contrasts or wall slip could help control microswimmer trapping and transport near microfluidic boundaries.
method: Represent the microswimmer using a two-dimensional point-singularity model.
Use complex-variable methods to derive explicit motion equations near a flat viscosity interface and a Navier-slip wall.
Analyse dynamical regimes as viscosity ratio or relative slip length varies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results identify three viscosity-controlled regimes and a periodic hydrodynamic bound state with zero net displacement; the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The idealised swimmer does not self-propel in unbounded fluid, and its two-dimensional dynamics require validation before application to real three-dimensional swimmers.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamics of a two-dimensional microswimmer near a slippery boundary

title: Computational performance versus numerical accuracy in the acoustic terms of weakly-compressible SPH
authors: Giuseppe Bilotta, Alireza Zarei, Roberta Cristofaro, Alexis Hérault, Élie Saikali, Morteza Derakhti
abstract: Accurate computation of the acoustic terms in weakly-compressible SPH, including the equation of state, its inverse, and the evaluation of the local speed of sound, is essential to ensure energy conservation, robust solid boundary conditions, and correct open boundary behavior. In the classic Cole's equation of state, using values of the polytropic constant $γ\ne 1$ can lead to significant precision loss, particularly when computations are performed in single precision, as is common in GPU implementations. We extend here our previous results on the optimal choice of state variable by introducing a new higher-precision form for all three acoustic terms, denoted \texttt{explog}, and assess its numerical accuracy and computational performance across a variety of devices and test cases. We find that the new form evaluates the acoustic terms with a maximum ULP of~2 for arguments less than $0.125$, and has higher errors in less than 1\% of the arguments larger than the threshold. Combined with a rewritten expression of the pressure at solid boundary particles in the ``dummy'' model, it provides consistently more accurate results, maintaining deviations from the reference pressure profile to below 2\%, even in presence of a rough bottom terrain. Computationally, the new formulation is also faster than the naive one on GPU, and only marginally slower on CPU.

infographic.key_insight: The explog formulation improves acoustic-term accuracy in weakly-compressible SPH while running faster than the naive formulation on GPU and only marginally slower on CPU.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate acoustic calculations support energy conservation and reliable solid and open boundary behavior in GPU-based SPH simulations.
method: Reformulate the equation of state, its inverse, and local sound speed using explog.
Rewrite pressure evaluation for dummy-model solid boundary particles.
Assess numerical accuracy and computational performance across devices and test cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a maximum error of 2 ULP for arguments below 0.125, higher errors for fewer than 1% of arguments above that threshold, and pressure-profile deviations below 2% even over rough terrain.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy is not uniformly bounded at 2 ULP above the reported threshold, and CPU evaluation incurs a small performance penalty.
infographic.paper_title: Computational performance versus numerical accuracy in the acoustic terms of weakly-compressible SPH

title: On Modelling the Scattering of Highly Nonlinear Transient Water Waves Due to Surface-Piercing Cylinder. Part I: Formulations and Verifications
authors: Qianyue Chen, Jinghua Wang, Daimeng Shang, Xianlong Lin
abstract: The presence of extreme ocean waves poses substantial threats to the safety of marine engineering applications and navigational activities. Accurate prediction of the nonlinear wave loads on offshore structures in large-diameter cylindrical configuration, such as monopile wind turbines and platform columns, requires a robust solution to the high-order wave diffraction problem. This paper introduces a novel, highly nonlinear time-domain numerical pseudo-spectrum model based on potential flow theory. By leveraging the Fredholm integral equation of the second kind and Legendre polynomials, a distinct efficient solver for computing the velocity potential on the cylinder surface and vertical velocity at free surface is developed. The present method is verified by comparing with a direct approach based on Fourier transform and established theoretical models for simulating the scattering of small steepness uniform waves. The convergence and computational efficiency of the present method is also demonstrated. The validation of the new model for simulating highly nonlinear transient water waves will be reported in Part II. The proposed model provides a powerful and efficient new framework for analyzing high-order nonlinear wave diffraction and hydrodynamic loads, with significant implications for both scientific research and the engineering design of coastal and offshore structures.

infographic.key_insight: A new nonlinear time-domain potential-flow model offers an efficient framework for predicting wave scattering by a surface-piercing cylinder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports wave-load analysis for large-diameter offshore structures such as wind-turbine monopiles and platform columns.
method: Represent nonlinear wave evolution with a time-domain pseudo-spectral model.
Use a second-kind Fredholm integral equation and Legendre polynomials.
Solve for cylinder-surface velocity potential and free-surface vertical velocity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Verification compares small-steepness uniform-wave scattering against a direct Fourier-transform approach and established theoretical models, with convergence and computational efficiency also demonstrated.
infographic.watch_item: Validation for highly nonlinear transient waves is deferred to Part II; this is a potential-flow solver, not an AI or turbulence model.
infographic.paper_title: On Modelling the Scattering of Highly Nonlinear Transient Water Waves Due to Surface-Piercing Cylinder. Part I: Formulations and Verifications
